To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
species persistence and community assemblage on islands and in isolated habitats is affected by species traits and habitat heterogeneity.

1) the lepidopteron community on an isolated habitat patch is dominated by generalist and mobile species; 2) the community composition of the isolated habitat patch differs from the mainland; 3) species traits (morphological, behavioural and ecological) are associated with species persistence and community composition on the isolated habitat patch.
the island-mainland situation acts as an ecological filter for the lepidopteron community and thus creates a specific subset of species that are adapted to the island situation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the lepidopteron communities on small islands and in the adjacent mainland are assembled.
the question how species composition and species persistence are affected by habitat fragmentation.
the long-term effects of habitat fragmentation on the persistence of species and the community assembly.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the island situation acts as an ecological filter, which selects only a subset of the lepidopteron species from the mainland.
species persistence in fragmented habitats depends on a complex interaction between species traits, habitat characteristics and the degree of isolation of the habitat.
island-mainland differences in lepidopterans are not only due to the distance to the mainland but also to differences in the habitat heterogeneity and species life-history traits.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
island-mainland lepidoptera assemblages are an excellent model system for species conservation in isolated habitat patches.
island-mainland differences in the lepidoptera community are mainly caused by differences in species composition, and not by changes in species richness or abundance.
the island situation creates an assembly of lepidopterans with a higher level of generalism, and that this is associated with a higher level in species richness.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the theory of island biogeo- graphy can be used to predict species persistence in isolated habitats, and that species traits can be used to test for the assembly of species communities.
the theory of island biogeo-raphy can be used as a blue-print for predicting species persistence and community composition in isolated habitat patches across landscapes.
species composition and persistence of lepidopterans in fragmented landscapes is determined by the interplay of life-history traits and the habitat structure.
